question_text: According to Uwais (2004), cited in the course material, as of September 2003 the number of Awaiting Trial inmates hovered between 60% and 75% of the total population of all incarcerated inmates in Nigerian detention institutions, amounting to how many inmates?
explanation: Uwais (2004) reported that as of September 2003, the number of Awaiting Trial inmates hovered between 60% and 75% of Nigeria's total incarcerated population, amounting to 40,082 inmates.

question_text: According to the course material, in the landmark case of Baye Johnson v. AG Lagos State and ANOR (2002), the Court of Appeal, per Galadima J.C.A., held that neither the Nigerian Constitution nor any other law in Nigeria provides for a Holding Charge, making the practice:
option_b: Fully constitutional and legally required in every case
option_c: A matter reserved exclusively for the Senate to decide
option_d: Applicable only to civil, not criminal, cases
explanation: In Baye Johnson v. AG Lagos State (2002), the Court of Appeal, per Galadima J.C.A., held that neither the Nigerian Constitution nor any other Nigerian law provides for a Holding Charge, making the practice unconstitutional.

question_text: According to Iwarimie-JaJa (2003), cited in the course material, civil disabilities imposed on convicted persons in a capitalist-oriented society like Nigeria include deprivation of the privilege to participate in political elections, hold public offices, obtain sensitive jobs and occupational licenses, and:
option_a: Obtaining different kinds of financial benefits, such as loans, insurance, and pension benefits
option_b: Access to any form of food or water while incarcerated
option_c: The ability to ever be released from custody under any circumstances
option_d: The right to breathe or move within their prison cell
explanation: Iwarimie-JaJa (2003) identifies civil disabilities including deprivation of the privilege to vote and hold public office, obtain sensitive jobs and licenses, enter legally enforceable instruments, and obtain financial benefits like loans, insurance, and pension benefits.

question_text: According to the course material, the statutory and regulatory system of civil disabilities imposed on convicted persons did not originate in Nigeria, but traces its origin to:
option_c: The Nigerian independence movement of 1960 exclusively
option_d: A concept with no historical precedent anywhere in the world
explanation: The course material notes that the Nigerian legal system did not originate the statutory system of civil disabilities; its origin was ancient Greece and Rome, later transmitted through English law, where convicted persons were considered "civilly dead".

question_text: According to Obiandu (2003), a Prison After Care Officer quoted in the course material, ex-prison inmates without tangible means of livelihood often return to motor parks, under flyovers, and waterfronts, where they may reclaim roles from within the prison subculture such as "cell provost" or:
explanation: Obiandu (2003) observed that ex-prison inmates without livelihoods return to high-criminality areas like motor parks and waterfronts, boasting of prison subculture roles such as cell provost, cell Chief Judge, cell Mopol, or cell IG.

question_text: According to the course material, recommendations from the 1990 National Conference on Prisons Reform included amnesty international's call for adoption of the body of principles under United Nations General Assembly Resolution 43/173, and Igweke and Gabriel's (1990) submission that crimes punishable with imprisonment should be replaced with other forms of:
option_b: Only capital punishment, with no alternative permitted
option_c: No punishment whatsoever, under any circumstances
option_d: Punishment applied exclusively to first-time offenders
explanation: At the 1990 National Conference on Prisons Reform, Igweke and Gabriel (1990) submitted that crimes punishable with imprisonment should be replaced with other forms of human punishment, alongside harmonising the Criminal and Penal Codes.

question_text: According to the course material, at the 1990 National Conference on Prisons Reform, Professor Eze of Abia State University argued that deprivation of liberty is a serious enough punishment in itself, stressing that prisoners' constitutional rights must be respected because "the fact of conviction does not define them out of:
explanation: Professor Eze argued at the 1990 conference that deprivation of liberty is a serious enough punishment, and prisoners' constitutional rights must be respected and enforced, since "the fact of conviction does not define them out of humanity".

question_text: According to the course material, Takaya and Egwu (1990), two political scientists at the 1990 National Conference on Prisons Reform, recommended the adoption of reform, re-socialization, rehabilitation, and re-integration as modern objectives of prisonization, alongside transforming Nigerian prisons into:
option_a: Organized training and employment centres commensurate with modern economy
option_b: Purely punitive facilities with no rehabilitative function whatsoever
option_c: Facilities exclusively for the death penalty
option_d: Institutions entirely closed to any form of government oversight
explanation: Takaya and Egwu (1990) recommended reform, re-socialization, rehabilitation, and re-integration as modern prisonization objectives, and the transformation of Nigerian prisons into organized training and employment centres commensurate with the modern economy.
